title: Chapter L

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth realizes Darcy is the man who would have suited her best, just as she believes the family disgrace has ended her chances. Wickham is to join the regulars in the north.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter L,” how does Austen show too late? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter L develops the idea of too late. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter L to complicate the reader's understanding of too late. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter L within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of too late responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter L as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of too late. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent philosophy. To be sure it would have been more for the advantage of conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the happiest alternative, been secluded from the world, in some distant farm house. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before, from all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband, her misery was considered certain.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Elizabeth recognize her love only now? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include precluding, eloping, regulars, subjoin, muslins. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “An union of a different tendency, and precluding the possibility of the other, was soon to be formed in their family.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To put a barrier before.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Austen often places realization at the point where hope seems lost. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's longing reflects her full change of heart. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent philosophy. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before, from all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband, her misery was considered certain.
